newsitem.title: USA: Rubin to mix tough words with warm on Asian trip.
newsitem.headline: Rubin to mix tough words with warm on Asian trip.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent

U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin sets off for Asia on Thursday on a six-day trip that is expected to start with tough talk for Japan on trade and wind up with words of support and friendship for Vietnam.

Rubin, who will also visit the Philippines for a meeting of Asia-Pacific finance ministers, sees the trip as a chance to strengthen ties with the world's fastest growing economic region and defend American interests there.
Speaking to reporters on Tuesday, the Treasury chief made clear that a renewed rise in Japan's trade surplus was not in interest of the United States or the world.
"They have made real progress (cutting the surplus) but the issue is not to have it go back the other way," he said.

Japan's trade surplus rose in February for the first time in two years, expanding by 6.5 percent from a year earlier, as the weak Japanese yen helped make the nation's exports more competitive on world markets.
U.S. officials have already warned Japan against trying to export its way out of its recent economic troubles and have urged it to spur domestic demand and thus boost its imports.

Washington is particularly concerned about Tokyo's plan to sharply tighten budget policy, fearing that a rise in consumption taxes that took effect on Tuesday will sap demand at home and force Japanese firms to look abroad for growth.

Rubin, who will meet Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto in Tokyo on Friday, will turn his attention to the regional economy on Saturday and Sunday when he attends a meeting of Asia-Pacific finance ministers in the Philippines.

U.S. officials said they expect the meeting, which will bring together policymakers from 18 economies, to highlight the consensus throughout the region on the need for sound, market-oriented economic policies, including privatisation.

The Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation group meeting will also discuss the so-called underpinnings needed for successful capital markets. That would include such issues as financial market regulation and supervision and investor protection.
While in the Philippines, Rubin is expected to hold bilateral meetings with the finance ministers from the host country and from China.

Rubin said he intended to raise the issue of alleged human rights abuses in China in his meeting with Chinese Finance Minister Liu Zhongli. "I can't imagine meeting with a Chinese official and not discussing human rights," he said.
Following the APEC meeting, Rubin will travel to Vietnam for a two day visit there.
He will be the highest-ranking U.S. economic policymaker to visit Vietnam in decades in the latest step toward normalising ties with America's former war-time foe.
"It seemed like a very good time to do something that would move this normalisation process forward," Rubin said, when asked why he chose to visit Vietnam at this time.

While in Hanoi, Rubin will sign an agreement to reschedule some $145 million of debts run up by the former government of South Vietnam and will discuss what other steps the two countries can take to normalise relations.
"There are very tangible things we need to do to move forward the normalisation process," a U.S. official said.
He did not elaborate. But Vietnam wants to be declared eligible for U.S. government export credits and most favoured nation trading privileges.
The official, who declined to be named, said that Vietnam was early in process of becoming a modern economy but looks to have favourable economic prospects in the long run.
